about: All-sky Hierarchical Progressive Surveys (HiPS) used by surveys.html, ordered from the longest wavelength (radio) to the shortest (gamma rays). 'hips' is what Aladin Lite is given: a CDS HiPS identifier (verified in the CDS HiPS registry, alasky MocServer or the HiPS list built into Aladin Lite 3.8.2). 'fallback' is tried if the first one cannot be loaded. log10m = log10 of a representative wavelength in metres, for the spectrum diagram. Tiles stream at run time from the providers' servers.

bands.name: Haslam 408 MHz
bands.instrument: Jodrell Bank Mark I (76 m), Effelsberg (100 m) and Parkes (64 m) radio telescopes
bands.year: Observed in the 1960s and 1970s, published 1982; destriped and source-subtracted map 2015
bands.reveals: Synchrotron radiation: electrons moving at nearly the speed of light spiralling around the Galaxy's magnetic field. The bright band is the Milky Way's disc; the great arc rising from the plane is the North Polar Spur, an old shell blown by supernovae and stellar winds.
bands.credit: Haslam et al. 1982 (A&AS 47, 1); Remazeilles et al. 2015 (MNRAS 451, 4311); HiPS by CDS

bands.name: Planck LFI colour
bands.instrument: European Space Agency (ESA) Planck, Low Frequency Instrument (LFI)
bands.reveals: Away from the Milky Way, the mottled pattern is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB): light released 380,000 years after the Big Bang, cooled to 2.7 kelvin. Along the plane, synchrotron and 'free–free' radio emission from ionised gas take over.
bands.credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration; HiPS by CDS

bands.name: Planck HFI colour
bands.instrument: ESA Planck, High Frequency Instrument (HFI), bolometers cooled to 0.1 kelvin
bands.reveals: The coldest dust in the Galaxy, at about 15–20 kelvin. Wispy 'cirrus' clouds reach far above the Milky Way's plane; the densest filaments are where the next generation of stars will form.
bands.credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration; HiPS by CDS

bands.name: AKARI FIS colour
bands.instrument: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) AKARI, Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS)
bands.reveals: Dust warmed to 20–40 kelvin by starlight. Star-forming regions glow white-hot here; the colour shifts toward blue where dust is warmer, as around young massive stars.
bands.credit: JAXA/ISAS AKARI; Doi et al. 2015 (PASJ 67, 50); HiPS by CDS

bands.name: AllWISE colour
bands.instrument: NASA Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), 40 cm telescope
bands.reveals: Blue and green show starlight from cool old stars, which shines straight through dust. Red (22 µm) is dust heated to 100–300 kelvin around newborn stars, and the soot-like Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) molecules that outline star-forming bubbles.

bands.name: 2MASS colour
bands.instrument: Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS): twin 1.3 m telescopes at Mount Hopkins, Arizona and Cerro Tololo, Chile
bands.reveals: Stars, almost half a billion of them. Near-infrared light slips through dust about ten times better than visible light, so the crowded bulge around the Galactic Centre appears where the eye sees only dark lanes.
bands.credit: 2MASS (University of Massachusetts and IPAC/Caltech, NASA and NSF); HiPS by CDS

bands.name: Finkbeiner H-alpha
bands.instrument: Composite of the Wisconsin H-Alpha Mapper (WHAM), Virginia Tech Spectral-line Survey (VTSS) and Southern H-Alpha Sky Survey Atlas (SHASSA)
bands.reveals: Hydrogen atoms re-forming after ultraviolet light from hot stars ripped them apart. As the electron drops from the third to the second energy level it emits this single red line, tracing HII regions, Barnard's Loop in Orion and the vast Gum Nebula.
bands.credit: Finkbeiner 2003 (ApJS 146, 407); WHAM, VTSS, SHASSA; HiPS by CDS

bands.name: Mellinger colour
bands.instrument: Axel Mellinger's all-sky mosaic of about 3,000 digital camera frames from South Africa, Texas and Michigan
bands.reveals: The sky roughly as your eye would see it from a very dark site: the glowing star clouds of the Milky Way, split by the Great Rift, a lane of dust that blocks the stars behind it.
bands.credit: Axel Mellinger (2009, PASP 121, 1180); HiPS by CDS

bands.name: DSS2 colour
bands.instrument: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (DSS2): Palomar Observatory Sky Survey (POSS-II) and UK Schmidt photographic plates, scanned by the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI)
bands.reveals: The deep, sharp optical sky on glass plates: stars to about magnitude 21, thousands of galaxies, and the glowing red gas and blue reflection nebulae around young stars.
bands.credit: DSS2: Caltech/Palomar, AAO/UKSTU, ESO, STScI (AURA/NASA); HiPS by CDS

bands.name: GALEX colour
bands.instrument: NASA Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX), 50 cm telescope
bands.reveals: Hot, young, massive stars, a few million years old, lighting up the spiral arms of galaxies, and white dwarfs. The Milky Way's plane is mostly missing: its bright stars could have damaged the detectors, so GALEX avoided it.

bands.name: eROSITA-DE DR1 colour
bands.instrument: extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) on the Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) spacecraft
bands.year: First all-sky survey (eRASS1) 2019–2020; German half released 2024
bands.reveals: Gas at millions of kelvin: supernova remnants, hot bubbles around the Galactic Centre, hot gas filling clusters of galaxies, and accreting black holes. This release covers only half the sky (Galactic longitudes 180°–360°), so half the map is empty.
bands.credit: eROSITA-DE DR1, Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE); Merloni et al. 2024 (A&A 682, A34)

bands.name: Fermi LAT colour
bands.instrument: NASA Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, Large Area Telescope (LAT)
bands.reveals: Cosmic rays, protons from supernova shocks, smashing into interstellar gas and making gamma rays. The plane glows where gas is densest; bright dots are pulsars and distant blazars, jets from supermassive black holes pointed at us.
bands.credit: NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration; HiPS by CDS

tour.name: Orion Nebula
tour.note: The nearest big stellar nursery, 1,340 light-years away. In visible light the glowing gas is lit by the four hot Trapezium stars at its heart. Switch to near-infrared and hundreds of young stars still wrapped in dust appear; in the mid-infrared the dust itself glows, showing the cavity those stars have carved into the molecular cloud behind.

tour.name: Andromeda Galaxy
tour.note: Our nearest large neighbour, 2.5 million light-years away. The optical view is dominated by the smooth glow of old stars in the bulge. Ultraviolet shows where stars were born in the last few hundred million years, strung along the spiral arms, and the mid-infrared reveals the famous 'ring of fire', a ring of warm dust 30,000 light-years from the centre.

tour.name: The Galactic Centre
tour.note: Looking toward the heart of our own Galaxy, 26,000 light-years away. In visible light dust clouds hide most of the bulge. Near-infrared light cuts through, revealing the peanut-shaped bar of old stars. In gamma rays the whole disc glows where cosmic rays strike gas, and above and below the centre lie the faint Fermi bubbles, relics of an outburst millions of years ago.

tour.name: Crab Nebula
tour.note: The debris of a star seen to explode in 1054 by Chinese and Japanese astronomers. The visible filaments are gas thrown out at 1,500 km/s. At its centre a pulsar, a neutron star spinning 30 times a second, powers a nebula of fast electrons that shines from radio waves to gamma rays; in X-rays that inner engine outshines everything else.

tour.name: Pleiades
tour.note: A young cluster about 100 million years old, 440 light-years away. The blue haze is not left over from the stars' birth: the cluster is drifting through an unrelated dust cloud, which reflects their light. Hot blue B stars blaze in ultraviolet, while the mid-infrared shows the dust being heated and pushed aside.

tour.name: Carina Nebula
tour.note: One of the largest star-forming regions in the Milky Way, four times the size of the Orion Nebula and 7,500 light-years away. Dozens of stars heavier than 50 Suns live here. Their winds collide and heat gas to millions of kelvin, which is why the whole region glows in X-rays; the mid-infrared traces dusty pillars eaten away by that radiation.

tour.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
tour.note: A satellite galaxy 160,000 light-years away, visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere. The visible view shows its stellar bar. Hydrogen-alpha picks out its star-forming regions, above all the Tarantula Nebula, the most active in the Local Group. Far-infrared shows the cool dust clouds that feed it.

tour.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
tour.note: A grand-design spiral 31 million light-years away, interacting with its small companion NGC 5195. The companion's gravity squeezes the spiral arms, triggering star formation, so the arms blaze in ultraviolet from massive young stars. In the mid-infrared the dust lanes along the inner edges of the arms glow.

tour.name: Sombrero Galaxy
tour.note: A galaxy seen almost edge-on, 31 million light-years away. In visible light a dark dust lane cuts across a huge bright bulge. Near-infrared shows mostly the smooth bulge of old stars, while at 22 µm the dust ring itself glows, revealing that it is a separate ring, not a spiral pattern.

tour.name: Cygnus Loop
tour.note: The expanding shell of a supernova that exploded 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, 2,400 light-years away and six Full Moons across. Where the blast wave hits interstellar clouds, the gas is shocked and glows in thin filaments. GALEX sees the whole shell in ultraviolet as a nearly complete bubble.

tour.name: Eta Carinae
tour.note: A pair of massive stars, the larger around 100 times the Sun's mass, 7,500 light-years away. In the 1840s it erupted and briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky, throwing off the two-lobed Homunculus Nebula. The winds of the two stars collide at thousands of kilometres per second and glow brightly in X-rays.

tour.name: Horsehead Nebula
tour.note: A dark pillar of dust and gas silhouetted against the glowing red emission nebula IC 434, about 1,400 light-years away. In visible light it is a black shape. In the near-infrared the dust thins and background stars start to show; in the mid-infrared its outer skin, heated by the star σ Orionis, glows.

tour.name: Cassiopeia A
tour.note: The youngest known supernova remnant in the Milky Way, 11,000 light-years away; its light reached Earth around 1680 with hardly anyone noticing, as dust dimmed it. In optical images there is almost nothing to see here. At 408 MHz it is the brightest radio source in the sky beyond the Sun, a bright spot in the Milky Way's band.

tour.name: M87 and the Virgo Cluster
tour.note: M87 is a giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of the Virgo Cluster, 54 million light-years away, whose black hole was the first ever imaged (2019). In optical light the cluster is a scatter of galaxies. In X-rays the space between them is filled with gas at tens of millions of kelvin. At radio wavelengths the jet from M87's black hole makes it one of the brightest sources in the sky.

tour.name: Ring Nebula
tour.note: A planetary nebula: the outer layers of a Sun-like star, puffed off at the end of its life, 2,600 light-years away. The white dwarf left at the centre is at over 100,000 kelvin and shines strongly in ultraviolet. The ring we see is a shell glowing because that ultraviolet light ionises it.

tour.name: Eagle Nebula
tour.note: Home of the Pillars of Creation, 7,000 light-years away. The young cluster NGC 6611 is eroding the surrounding cloud with ultraviolet light and winds. Near-infrared shows stars behind and inside the pillars; mid-infrared shows the dust at the cloud's surface being heated.

tour.name: Rho Ophiuchi clouds
tour.note: One of the closest star-forming clouds, about 460 light-years away, next to the red supergiant Antares. To the eye it is a tangle of colourful reflection nebulae and dark lanes. In the infrared the dark lanes turn bright: they are the densest, coldest dust, where hundreds of young stars are forming right now.

tour.name: Coma Cluster
tour.note: A rich cluster of more than 1,000 galaxies, 320 million light-years away. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky measured how fast its galaxies move and found that far more mass must be present than we can see: the first evidence for dark matter. Most of its ordinary matter is hot gas that shines in X-rays, in the half of the sky this X-ray release does not include.

tour.name: Hubble Deep Field
tour.note: In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared for ten days at this empty-looking spot in Ursa Major, a patch about the size of a tennis ball seen from 100 metres. It found about 3,000 galaxies, some seen as they were over 12 billion years ago. The all-sky surveys here barely show anything: that is the point of a deep field.

tour.name: Sagittarius A*
tour.note: The Milky Way's central black hole, 4 million times the Sun's mass. Visible light from here is dimmed by about 30 magnitudes (a factor of a trillion) by dust, so the optical image shows almost nothing. In the near-infrared the dimming falls to about 2.5 magnitudes, and the densest star cluster in the Galaxy appears, crowded around the black hole.
